### Brief Hospital Course

##### Primary Diagnosis: Abdominal Pain Other Specified (ICD-10 title: ABDPAIN-OTHER)

The patient, a __ year old female with a past medical history of Breast Cancer (Stage I), Hypertension, and Hypothyroidism, presented with chief complaints of abdominal pain and bloody stools. Upon initial presentation, vital signs included temperature 98.1°F, heart rate 88 bpm, respiration rate 18 breaths/minute, oxygen saturation 99%, blood pressure 138/91 mmHg, and pain score 5/10.

On examination, there was bright red blood observed in the vagina. Subsequent computed tomography (CT) scan revealed segmental colitis of the distal transverse and proximal descending colon, which was most likely due to ischemia based on the watershed distribution and association with bright red blood per rectum. Infectious or inflammatory etiologies of colitis were considered less likely. Additionally, an ultrasound of the aorta and its branches did not show any evidence of hemodynamically significant stenosis within the aorta, SMA, or Celiac axis.

Throughout the hospital stay, the patient received treatment including ciprofloxacin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and atenolol. Laboratory results indicated elevated white blood cell count (12.7 x 10^3 cells/mcL) and lactic acid levels (1.9 mmol/L). However, tests for Clostridioides difficile (CDiff) were negative.

At the time of discharge, the patient reported improvement in their symptoms and denied current nausea or vomiting. Physical examination revealed soft and non-distended abdomen with active bowel sounds. The patient was discharged with continued medication regimen consisting of atenolol, levothyroxine sodium, and venlafaxine extended release.

The patient was advised to schedule a colonoscopy in the near future to complete the evaluation of the colitis. Further management and follow-up care were not specified in the discharge summary.</s>

# Chief complaint: Subternal chest pain

## Cardiovascular system

Upon arrival, vital signs revealed a temperature of 97.7°F, pulse rate of 74 bpm, respiratory rate of 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation of 99%, systolic blood pressure of 171 mmHg, and diastolic blood pressure of 97 mmHg. The patient reported a pain score of 4 on a scale of 10, with acuity rated at 2.0. The portable chest X-ray showed no evidence of acute cardiopulmonary process.

## Major interventions and procedures

Consultation with Atrius Cardiology was sought, recommending two sets and a stress test.

## Progress during hospital stay

In the emergency department, initial vital signs remained relatively stable, with slight improvements observed upon transfer to the ward (BP 140/82 mmHg, HR 70 bpm). The patient was asymptomatic throughout their hospitalization.

## Past medical history

The patient has a history of hypertension, bipolar disorder, blindness, albinism, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), tobacco abuse, obesity, psoriasis, restless leg syndrome, umbilical hernia repair, and laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Notably, there is no history of diabetes or dyslipidemia.

## Family history

Significant family members include a father with prostate cancer, a mother who passed away at an unknown age from a potential pulmonary embolism, a maternal grandmother who also died from a suspected pulmonary embolism, and a brother who experienced a deep vein thrombosis after a long flight.

## Physical examination

Initial and final physical examinations were largely unremarkable, with some observations including distention of the abdomen at baseline, presence of 2+ edema bilaterally up to the knees, and a groin erythema and rash.

## Laboratory results

Notable laboratory findings included white blood cell count of 8.6 K/μL, hemoglobin of 14.6 g/dL, platelet count of 282 K/μL, creatinine of 1.0 mg/dL, and a negative troponin result twice.

## Imaging studies

An electrocardiogram stress test revealed diffuse 1-2 mm horizontal/downsloping ST segment depression in leads I, II, III, avF, V3-V6, and 0.5-1 mm ST segment elevation in leads avR, avL, and possibly V1, starting early within one minute of exercise onset and persisting through recovery. Additionally, a cardiac perfusion scan and echocardiography were performed, revealing mild global hypokinesis with an ejection fraction of 40%.</s>

He underwent Mohs excisions for forehead, right ear, and back basal cell and squamous cell carcinomas. Upon arrival in the ED, his blood pressure was persistently high (>190/100mmHg), leading to administration of antihypertensives. However, he became bradycardic and hypotensive, requiring additional interventions. During hospitalization, his vital signs stabilized, and he reported head pain related to surgical site.

------------------

Interventions & Treatments
---------------------------
Hypertension management included intravenous metoprolol, hydralazine, and glucagon to counteract the effects of beta blockers. Pain management involved administering analgesics for surgical site pain.

Clinical Progress
-----------------
Initially, the patient experienced symptoms such as dizziness, weakness, and nausea. Over time, his vital signs stabilized, allowing him to become ambulatory again. By the end of the hospital stay, he was alert, oriented, and free of acute distress.

We are pleased to inform you that you are being discharged from our care today. During your stay, you were diagnosed with an abdominal stab wound with mesenteric root bleed. To aid in your recovery, we performed a surgery which included a cytolomy and small bowel resection. We also administered several interventions including intravenous fluids, antibiotics, and pain management.

Here are some guidelines to help you manage at home:

1. Pain Management: Continue taking oxycodone liquid 5 mg PO Q4H PRN for pain relief. Be cautious about driving or operating machinery while taking this medication.

2. Constipation Prevention: Take senna 2 tab PO BID PRN for constipation prevention.

3. Monitor Your Recovery: Keep track of your temperature, heart rate, and any signs of infection such as redness, swelling, or increased pain around the surgical site. Contact us immediately if you notice any concerning symptoms.

Important Phone Numbers:
- Emergency Room: (XXX) XXX-XXXX
- Primary Care Physician: (XXX) XXX-XXXX

Return Appointment:
It's essential to schedule a follow-up appointment with your primary care physician within two weeks of discharge to ensure proper healing and address any concerns.

Please contact us if you have any questions or need assistance setting up your follow-up appointment.

Best Regards,
[Your Surgery Team]</s>

This patient was admitted due to Respiratory Distress related to Pulmonary Congestion. During their stay, they underwent Coronary Artery Bypass Graft surgery (CABG) with the use of the left internal mammary artery and a saphenous vein graft. Additionally, endoscopic harvesting of the long saphenous vein was performed.

While recovering from the procedure, it is essential to take the following steps:

1. Take prescribed medication as directed. This includes Aspirin, Metformin, Metoprolol, Ranitidine, Vitamin D, Tramadol, Oxycodone-Acetaminophen, Hydralazine, Docusate Sodium, Atorvastatin, Furosemide, and Potassium Chloride. 4. No driving for approximately one month and while taking narcotic pain relievers.

5. Keep incision sites clean and dry. Do not apply lotions, creams, powders, or ointments to the incisions unless instructed otherwise by your doctor.

6. Shower daily, using gentle soap to wash incisions. Avoid baths or swimming until cleared by your physician.

7. Check temperatures each morning and evening and record readings.

The patient, a ____ female, presented with symptoms of respiratory distress and chest pain. Upon admission, she exhibited signs of pulmonary congestion and hypostasis, as indicated by a chest radiograph showing mild ground-glass opacity in the right lung, a slightly enlarged heart, and mild pulmonary vascular congestion/interstitial edema.

Initially treated with nitrates, furosemide, and noninvasive positive pressure ventilation, the patient's condition stabilized. Subsequently, she was diagnosed with three-vessel coronary artery disease through cardiac catheterization. As a result, she underwent urgent coronary artery bypass graft x3; left internal mammary artery to left anterior descending artery, and saphenous vein graft to ramus and the distal right coronary arteries. Additionally, endoscopic harvesting of the long saphenous vein was performed.

Throughout her hospital stay, the patient's vital signs remained relatively stable, with improvements observed in her lung volumes. However, there were instances of minor complications such as a small left pleural effusion detected in various imaging studies. These issues were addressed accordingly, and the patient's internal jugular central venous catheter was adjusted to ensure proper placement.

Eventually, the patient was deemed ready for discharge, presenting in a stable condition with improved respiratory function, ambulation, and manageable sternal pain. Her discharge diagnosis included diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, CAD with 2 prior MIs, congestive heart failure, CVA with right-sided weakness, asthma, GERD, past cholecystectomy, and past cardiac procedures consisting of 3 stents placed at specific dates.

She was discharged home with appropriate follow-up instructions and prescribed medications including aspirin, fluticasone propionate, metformin, ranitidine, vitamin D, tramadol, oxycodone-acetaminophen, metoprolol tartrate, hydralazine, docusate sodium, atorvastatin, furosemide, potassium chloride, and albuterol inhaler.</s>

An upright AP and lateral view of the chest confirmed the correct positioning of a right-sided nerve stimulator device.

Her physical examination indicated normal vital signs, intact cranial nerves, and full motor function with no pronounced tremors or abnormal movements. Sensation testing yielded normal results as well.

Despite these issues, the patient was discharged in a non-focal state with a clear and coherent mental status, maintaining an alert and interactive level of consciousness. She was ambulatory and independent.

Her medication regimen included gabapentin, levothyroxine sodium, methadone, topiramate, acetaminophen-caffeine-butalbital combination, and hydromorphone for breakthrough pain management.

Upon discharge, no specific follow-up instructions were mentioned in the discharge report.</s>

### Brief Hospital Course:

#### Chief complaint: Left brow pain and swelling

On presentation, the patient exhibited left brow pain and swelling, which was attributed to an allergic reaction. This was accompanied by mild pain on the left side of her head, poor peripheral vision in her left eye, and dry feeling in the left eye.

Initial interventions included administration of Ondansetron for nausea, Epinephrine for severe allergic reactions, Prazosin, Acetaminophen, BuPropion, and Propranolol for various symptoms such as anxiety, pain, and headaches. Additionally, Metronidazole topical gel was applied twice daily to treat any potential bacterial infections, and bisacodyl was administered daily to manage constipation.

A CT scan of the sinus, mandible, and maxillofacial region was performed to evaluate for fluid collections. Findings revealed mild fat stranding overlying the left zygoma, with no focal collection or acute fractures observed.

Throughout the hospital stay, the patient received numerous medications, including Aripiprazole, Azathioprine, Bisacodyl, Buprenorphine, BuPropion, Carisoprodol, Colchicine, Cyanocobalamin, Desmopressin, Desvenlafaxine, Docusate sodium, Fluticasone nasal spray, Fluticasone-Salmeterol diskus, Hydroxyzine, Ipratropium bromide, Levothyroxine, Lorazepam, Metronidazole topical gel, Montelukast, Multivitamins, Ondansetron, Prazosin, Prednisone, Propranolol, Quetiapine, Ranitidine, Sumatriptan, and Valacyclovir. Abatacept was also administered every four weeks.

As the patient improved, the focus shifted towards managing ongoing conditions such as bipolar disorder, borderline personality disorder, dissociative identity disorder, fibromyalgia, chronic seronegative inflammatory arthropathy, chronic kidney disease, GERD, and migraines.

At discharge, the patient showed clear and coherent mental status, remained alert and interactive, and ambulated independently. The primary diagnosis was facial contusion.</s>

### Brief Hospital Course

#### Initial Presentation

The patient, a 57-year-old female, presented with complaints of dyspnea and right leg swelling. Upon arrival, vital signs included temperature 96.9°F, heartrate 92.0 bpm, resprate 18.0 bpm, o2sat 100.0%, sbp 117.0 mmHg, dbp 62.0 mmHg, and pain score 0. The chief complaint was dyspnea and right leg swelling.

#### Investigations and Findings

An initial portable AP chest radiograph revealed mild cardiomegaly, smoothly marginated opacity within the mid to lower left lung consistent with a known loculated effusion, dense left basilar atelectasis, no evidence of pneumothorax, and diffuse bilateral parenchymal nodularity. A subsequent chest (portable AP) showed slight interval increase in ill-defined opacities at the right lung base.

A CT chest with contrast identified stable bilateral pulmonary nodules and pleural nodularity consistent with metastatic disease, persistent loculated left pleural effusion, and no evidence of pulmonary embolism or aortic abnormality. Additionally, there appeared to be interval increase in ill-defined opacities at the right lung base.

A chest ultrasound did not demonstrate significant increase in the patient's prior pleural effusions.

#### Interventions and Treatment

No invasive procedures were performed during this admission. The patient was managed conservatively with oxygen supplementation and diuretics.

#### Progress During Admission

Despite treatment, the patient continued to experience dyspnea and developed mild chest pain related to her prior chest tube sites. There were no reported fevers or chills. Bedside thoracic ultrasound did not reveal significant increases in her prior pleural effusions.

#### Discharge Summary

The patient was discharged with prescriptions for guaifenesin, ipratropium-albuterol nebulizer solution, lorazepam, oxycodone sustained release, simethicone, and acetaminophen. The primary diagnosis was acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, secondary to metastatic pancreatic cancer. The patient was discharged in a stable mental state, able to walk with assistance or aid, and scheduled for follow-up appointments as necessary.</s>

### Dizziness Episode

##### Initial Evaluation

This __ y/o F with a medical history of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), renal transplant, and prior Deep Venous Thrombosis (DVT), presented with complaints of dizziness. Upon initial examination, vital signs were within normal limits except for an elevated D-dimer. Due to a contrast allergy, a Bedside Lower Extremity Ultrasound (BLE US) was conducted to rule out potential DVT.

##### Ultrasound Findings

The ultrasound revealed normal compressibility, flow, and augmentation in the bilateral common femoral, femoral, and popliteal veins. There was also no evidence of deep venous thrombosis in either lower extremity.

##### Subsequent Events

In the Emergency Department (ED), the patient received multiple medications for symptom relief, including Lorazepam, Mirtazapine, Prazosin, Ziprasidone, Acyclovir, Hydroxychloroquine, Metoprolol, Prednisone, Tacrolimus, and additional medications. Despite these interventions, the patient reported persistent lightheadedness and mental fogginess upon transfer to the medicine unit. On arrival, there was also mild calf tenderness on the right side and rib pain with coughing or deep breathing.

##### Further Investigations

Additional laboratory tests were ordered, which included complete blood count, glucose, electrolytes, creatinine, calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, troponin T, and D-dimer. The results of these tests were not specified in the discharge summary.

##### Progress During Admission

Over the course of hospitalization, the patient's vital signs remained mostly stable, with slight variations in temperature, blood pressure, and heart rate. Physical examination throughout the admission period indicated no abnormalities, apart from mild calf tenderness on the right side.

##### Discharge Summary

At the time of discharge, the patient felt somewhat improved but still experienced lingering lightheadedness and mental fogginess. The cause of these symptoms remains undetermined based on the information provided in the discharge summary. The patient was discharged with a diagnosis of dizziness, and the prescribed medications included Acyclovir, Clindamycin, Epinephrine, Hydroxychloroquine, Lorazepam, Metoprolol, Mirtazapine, Prazosin, Prednisone, Tacrolimus, and Vitamin D.</s>

Upon arrival, vital signs included temperature 98.4°F, heartrate 89 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 95%, systolic blood pressure 107 mmHg, diastolic blood pressure 58 mmHg, and pain score 6/10. The chief complaint was cough, syncope, weakness, dyspnea on exertion, dizziness.

On initial evaluation, a CXR revealed bilateral pneumonia and suspected interstitial lung disease. Subsequent CTA chest confirmed these findings, revealing bilateral ground-glass opacities with subpleural reticulation, reticular opacities, and thickening of bronchovascular bundles, most suggestive of a fibrotic subtype nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP). Additionally, a small hiatal hernia was noted.

The patient was hospitalized and treated with IV ceftriaxone and azithromycin. During the hospital stay, the patient reported improved exercise tolerance but continued cough persisted. Pulmonary function tests and outpatient pulmonology follow-up were recommended upon discharge.

Medications prescribed at discharge include clobetasol propionate cream, doxazosin, finasteride, a mucous membrane solution for pain relief, levofloxacin, and a prescription for the latter medication (Levaquin). The patient was discharged home with a diagnosis of community-acquired pneumonia and interstitial lung disease. At discharge, the patient was alert and interactive, ambulating independently, and clear in thought processes. Follow-up appointments were recommended.</s>

Electrocardiogram was unremarkable, and enzyme levels were negative. Upon diagnosis of subsegmental left basilar atelectasis, the patient received sublingual nitroglycerin, morphine 4mg IV, insulin human 70/30 (unknown dosage), and was transferred to the Cardiology service for chest pain management.

# Pulmonary Event:
Upon arrival to the ward, the patient reported comfort, mild chest heaviness 1.5/10, and no new symptoms. A chest X-ray revealed low lung volumes, normal heart size, and mediastinal and hilar contours. Linear opacities within the left lung base were consistent with subsegmental atelectasis. No focal consolidation, pleural effusion, or pneumothorax was detected.
